usage: Goes right before the verb; the most basic way to say 'a lot'
Handy when ordering food or asking for more
With adjectives 많이 can mean 'very', like 'a lot busy'
너무 많이 마셨어요 = I drank too much
examples: 비가 오다 = it rains; 많이 shows the amount
I like Korean food a lot.
Put 많이 before 좋아해요 to say 'like a lot'
Please eat a lot / Enjoy your meal.
A warm, common thing hosts say at the table
nuance: 많이 is the everyday word for 'a lot/much' and sits right in front of the verb it describes, such as 많이 먹어요 or 많이 자요. With feelings or states it can also mean 'very', so 많이 아파요 means 'it hurts a lot'. It is one of the first adverbs a beginner should learn because it works for both amount and degree.
mistakes: Using the adjective 많다 where you need the adverb 많이; before a verb you say 많이 먹어요, not 많다 먹어요.
Putting 많이 after the verb; in Korean the adverb comes before the verb, so 먹어요 많이 sounds wrong.

english: a little, a bit, a few
usage: The opposite of 많이; asks for a small amount
With adjectives it softens the degree to 'a bit'
조금만 기다려 주세요 = please wait just a moment
Means 'a moment ago', a fixed time phrase
examples: Perfect modest answer for a beginner
조금 before the verb shows a small amount
조금 softens 피곤해요 to 'a bit tired'
nuance: 조금 means 'a little / a bit' and is the natural partner to 많이 for small amounts or mild degrees. In fast speech it very often shrinks to 좀, so 조금만요 and 좀만요 are the same idea. It is gentle and polite, which makes it useful for softening requests and modest answers like 조금 해요.
mistakes: Forgetting that 조금 usually becomes 좀 in casual speech; both are correct, but 좀 sounds more conversational.
Using 조금 for large amounts; it only ever means a small degree, so 조금 많이 is contradictory.

usage: The short, spoken form of 조금
좀 also softens requests, like a gentle 'please'
Very common when ordering or asking for things
examples: It's a bit cold in here.
좀 makes the comment sound soft and casual
Adding 좀 makes a request more polite and natural
좀 softens the refusal so it sounds friendly
nuance: 좀 is the shortened, spoken version of 조금 and is everywhere in daily conversation. Besides meaning 'a little', it works as a softener that makes requests gentler and more polite, much like adding 'please' in English. So 물 주세요 is fine, but 물 좀 주세요 sounds warmer and more natural.
mistakes: Thinking 좀 only means 'a little'; in requests it mainly works as a politeness softener, not an amount.
Using 좀 in very formal writing, where the full 조금 or a polite request form fits better.

usage: Right before the verb; means the action is complete
Everything is good / I like it all
I did it all / I'm done
Very common to report finishing a task
거의 다 왔어요 = we're almost there
examples: 다 + 했어요 means the whole thing is done
Common at the table when your plate is empty
nuance: 다 is a small but powerful word meaning 'all / everything / completely', placed right before the verb. It can describe finishing an action fully (다 했어요 = all done) or covering everyone or everything (다 왔어요 = everyone came). Because it is short and extremely frequent, beginners hear it constantly in everyday speech.
mistakes: Confusing the adverb 다 (all) with 또 (again); they look short but mean different things.
Forgetting 다 goes before the verb; you say 다 먹었어요, not 먹었어요 다.

usage: A slightly fuller, clearer 'all/everyone' than 다
모두 합쳐서 얼마예요? = how much for everything?
모두 다 means 'all of them' with extra emphasis
examples: My family is four people in all.
모두 sums up a total number
A friendly greeting to a group
nuance: 모두 means 'all / everyone / in total' and feels a touch fuller and clearer than the very short 다. It can be a noun ('everyone': 모두 환영해요) or an adverb ('all': 모두 모였어요), so it is flexible. Use it when you want to address or count a whole group, like 가족이 모두 네 명 or 여러분 모두.
mistakes: Assuming 모두 only works as an adverb; it can also stand as a noun meaning 'everyone'.
Using 모두 only for people; it also works for things and totals, like 모두 합쳐서 (all together).

usage: A clear, slightly polite way to say 'together'
친구와 함께 = together with a friend
다 함께 노래해요 = let's all sing together
examples: Let's watch a movie together this weekend.
함께 before the verb means 'do it together'
I had dinner together with my family.
A friendly suggestion to a classmate
nuance: 함께 means 'together' and is a slightly warmer, more polished partner to the casual 같이. It often pairs with 와/과 to say 'together with someone', as in 친구와 함께. Both 함께 and 같이 are common, but 함께 sounds a touch softer and shows up often in invitations and announcements.
mistakes: Thinking 함께 and 같이 are totally different; they overlap closely, with 함께 just sounding a bit softer.
Forgetting the particle 와/과 before 함께 when naming the person, as in 친구와 함께.

english: just, simply, for no special reason
usage: I just feel kind of off
A vague, soft way to dodge a full explanation
examples: I just want to rest today.
For coffee, just an americano, please.
nuance: 그냥 means 'just / simply / for no particular reason' and is one of the most useful filler-style words in casual Korean. It can soften a statement (그냥 좀 그래요), mean 'plain/as-is' (그냥 주세요), or answer 'why?' with a light 'no reason' (그냥). Beginners hear it constantly, so recognizing it makes everyday speech much easier to follow.
mistakes: Treating 그냥 as having one fixed translation; its meaning shifts with context between 'just', 'plain', and 'no reason'.
Overusing it in formal settings; 그냥 is casual and can sound too vague in business writing.

usage: Adds a strong promise to the verb
examples: I'll be sure to call tomorrow.
꼭 makes the promise sound firm
Make sure to take your medicine.
Let's definitely go together next time.
nuance: 꼭 means 'definitely / without fail' and adds strong intention or a firm request to a sentence. With promises it sounds sincere (꼭 갈게요), and with requests it makes them warm but firm (꼭 오세요). It can also mean 'exactly/just like', as in 꼭 엄마 같아요, though the 'for sure' meaning is what beginners use most.
mistakes: Confusing 꼭 (for sure) with 곧 (soon); they look and sound similar but mean different things.
Using 꼭 for casual maybes; it implies real certainty or a firm wish, not 'perhaps'.

usage: 바로 앞에 있어요 = it's right in front
examples: The school is right next to my house.
바로 before the verb means immediately
nuance: 바로 has two everyday meanings: 'right away / immediately' with actions (바로 가요), and 'exactly / right (there)' with places and identifications (바로 여기, 바로 그거예요). For location it stresses something is directly next to or in front of a point, like 바로 옆 or 바로 앞. Context makes clear which meaning is intended, and both are very common for beginners.
mistakes: Assuming 바로 only means 'immediately'; it also means 'exactly/right' for places and things.
Placing 바로 far from the word it modifies; keep it right before the verb or noun, as in 바로 앞.

usage: The basic word for doing something fast
Repeated for emphasis; a famous Korean phrase
더 빨리 해 주세요 = please do it faster
examples: Hurry up, the bus is coming!
Everyday urging when in a rush
A caring set phrase to a sick person
nuance: 빨리 means 'quickly / fast' and is among the first action adverbs beginners need. Doubled as 빨리빨리, it captures the well-known Korean 'hurry, hurry' spirit and adds urgency. It pairs with almost any action verb (빨리 가요, 빨리 먹어요) and appears in warm set phrases like 빨리 나으세요 (get well soon).
mistakes: Mixing up the adverb 빨리 (quickly) with the adjective 빠르다 (to be fast); before a verb you use 빨리.
Using 빨리 to describe a noun; for 'a fast car' you need 빠른 차, not 빨리 차.

usage: A bit fuller and warmer than plain 더
A kind wish, slightly formal tone
examples: I'll work even harder from now on.
날씨가 더우니 물을 더욱 많이 마셔요.
Since it's hot, drink even more water.
After practicing, it got even better.
nuance: 더욱 means 'even more / all the more' and is a slightly fuller, warmer version of the basic 더. It often appears in sincere statements and good wishes, like 더욱 노력할게요 or 더욱 건강하세요, and the doubled 더욱더 adds extra emphasis. In very casual chat people just say 더, so save 더욱 for heartfelt or polished sentences.
mistakes: Assuming 더욱 is totally different from 더; they overlap, with 더욱 sounding fuller and a bit more formal.
Using 더욱 in very casual texting, where the shorter 더 sounds more natural.

usage: A warm, gentle 'really', softer than 너무
Sincere compliment with a kind tone
참 alone signals a sudden 'oh, that reminds me'
examples: The weather is really nice today.
참 gives a soft, sincere feeling
Your Korean pronunciation is really good.
Oh, by the way, are you free tomorrow?
참 as a 'that reminds me' opener
nuance: 참 means 'really / truly' with a gentle, sincere warmth, making it lovely for heartfelt compliments like 참 좋아요 or 참 예뻐요. It feels softer and kinder than the strong 너무 or 정말. As a standalone exclamation, 참! also works as 'oh, by the way!' when you suddenly remember something, so context tells you which sense applies.
mistakes: Reading every 참 as an intensifier; standing alone it often means 'oh, that reminds me!'.
Expecting 참 to sound strong; it is a soft, warm 'really', not a heavy emphasis like 너무.

usage: Describes filling something to the top
방이 사람으로 가득 찼어요 = the room is packed with people
가득 담아 주세요 = please fill it up
Common when getting gas: 가득이요 = full tank
examples: I poured the cup full of water.
The mart is full of people.
Useful at a gas station or when ordering
nuance: 가득 means 'fully / full to the brim' and describes a container, space, or feeling being completely filled. It pairs naturally with verbs like 채우다, 차다, 담다, and the form 가득하다 means 'to be full'. A handy real-life use is at the gas station, where 가득이요 means 'fill the tank, please'.
mistakes: Using 가득 for general 'a lot' with any verb; it specifically means 'filled full', so it fits filling and packing.
Mixing up 가득 (full to the brim) with 많이 (a lot in amount); they overlap but are not identical.

usage: 푹 쉬세요 = rest up well, a caring phrase
드라마에 푹 빠졌어요 = I'm hooked on the drama
examples: Please rest up well at home today.
A warm thing to say to a tired person
I slept soundly yesterday, so I feel refreshed.
For a cold, resting well is best.
nuance: 푹 means doing something deeply and thoroughly, and it shows up most in 푹 쉬다 (rest well) and 푹 자다 (sleep soundly), which beginners hear all the time as caring wishes. In cooking it means simmering thoroughly until soft, and figuratively 푹 빠지다 means 'to be totally hooked'. It is a vivid, friendly word that adds a sense of 'completely and comfortably'.
mistakes: Treating 푹 as a general 'very'; it specifically means deeply/soundly and fits resting, sleeping, and simmering.
Forgetting the very common set phrase 푹 쉬세요, the natural way to tell someone to rest up.
